lectures.title: The Logical Volume Manager (LVM): Flexible Storage Management

cues.en: We now already got a rough overview about the logical volume manager, and in this lecture we want to
have a look, a more detailed look at this.
The idea with the logical volume manager is that instead of placing our volume like our file system
and then what we mount directly on a disk or directly onto a partition of a disk, we can place a device
mapper in between.
This allows us to combine the space from multiple disks, and this space will then be provided to us
as a volume group.
How we create that one, how we manage it.
This will all be the contents of this chapter.
On top of this, we are then able to create our partitions.
Let's have a look at the schema here.
So here we got our drive and we might have there some partitions and then some file system on top that
would still be supported with llVM.
So llVM this would then be like, okay, llVM will not touch this part of the drive the way llVM works
on like the lowest level is that we say, okay, here we have a partition for llVM and all the space
there is managed by llVM.
So for example here we might have a traditional partition with a traditional volume on top of that.
But the main thing is that we have a space reserved for llVM here.
This is important for llVM this that we have a traditional partition with a traditional file system
on top how we have seen it before.
This is completely optional here in this course we have for now we will use the three drives at 50GB
first.
So for now we have completely clean, hard disks with no existing partitions there.
So we will be using all the space of those drives for llVM.
But just so you're aware, we could theoretically also have traditional partitions on those drives.
But the idea here is that we create a partition and we say, okay, here, this should now be reserved
for llVM, this storage space.
So we have an llVM terminology.
It's called physical volumes that would for example, be the partition sdb2 in a sense that we have
reserved that partition for llVM or if we have another drive and it's only used for llVM, that would
then be, for example, SDC one or SDD one.
So we have those physical volumes.
They are partitions on a hardware level and on top of those physical volumes we can place our volume
group, we can name that however we want, and V Group is the name that I will be using here in this
course because I feel like this name represents quite well that it's a volume group.
But in practice it would also be great if that name would represent what this volume group is doing.
But here all it's doing is to visualize the concept, how llVM works.
So that's why I will call my volume group just v group.
But the idea here is that we place this volume group on top of our physical volumes and this will then
act as like a container owner and into that volume group or into that container, we can then create
so-called logical volumes.
So for example, here we could create a volume with the name data or another one with the name backups,
and they are placed on top of this volume group and the volume group is then responsible for storing
it on the physical volumes.
And this allows us to have this abstraction in between that we are no longer directly accessing our
partitions, but there's this volume group in between and this allows us to have multiple drives for
the same logical volume here in our system.
So this is our setup with LVM.
How do we create a setup like this?
Well, we have to start at the bottom, so we have to first create a physical volume.
Then on top we can create a volume group.
And then on top of that, we can create a logical volume.
So the same will apply here in the course.
In the next lecture, we will start to first initialize our physical volumes.
